feedback: If row counts don't add up to the number of cards, a card may have been lost or double-counted — recount by moving each card aside as it is tallied, and check the parts sum to the whole
If asked 'which does the class like best?' and the child re-counts cards instead of reading the table, model reading it: 'the biggest number is beside…' and return to the question
If a card fits none of the given categories, don't force it into a pile — allow an 'other' category if genuinely needed
Point to each pile and its matching table row together as the number is written, so counts and labels stay correctly paired
activities.intendedInsight: An organised table is a tool that ANSWERS a question, not just a store of numbers: once ordered, the record visibly shows the most popular category, the totals should reconcile with the whole set, and updating a count updates the answer.
learnerActions: Start from a real question the class cares about, e.g. 'which of these three snacks is most popular?' or 'which of these three fruits does our class like best?'
Take a shuffled stack of class response cards and sort each card into one of 2-3 categories, building a tally as you go
Write each category name beside its count in a simple table or list
Check that the row counts add up to the number of cards you started with (e.g. '7 + 5 + 4 = 16, and we had 16 cards')
Order the categories from most to fewest so the category with the biggest count rises to the top (if two categories have the same biggest count, say that they are tied rather than naming one winner)
Read the table back aloud to state which category answers the question

Test the table as a live record: if two more children chose one fruit, update that count, check that the new total is 2 more than before (e.g. 18 instead of 16), and see whether the ordered answer changes
activities.title: Survey organiser: from response cards to a table that answers the question

feedback: If the child reads a count without naming its category, re-pair the label and number together
This reference-only reading supports interpretation but does not itself practise organising raw data — pair it with a hands-on sort so the child also builds the table
activities.intendedInsight: Reading a table back — pairing each label with its count and identifying the largest — is a necessary step toward using data to answer a question.
learnerActions: Look at a completed, labelled frequency table of category names and counts
Point to each row and say what it means ('this row says 5 children chose banana')
Say which row has the biggest count and what question that answers
activities.title: Read a completed table to say what it means (annotation scaffold)
